interactions.summary: The canto continues with the wounded Navarrese sinner naming other grafters, then offering to whistle more sinners out of hiding if the demons will momentarily stand back.

Jiang glosses the scene as fraud stacked on fraud: the sinner deceives demons who enjoy tearing people apart, the demons fall for it and crash into the pitch, and Jiang asks the class to name the deeper paradox behind that lie.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading with Jiang interpretation and prompt

claims.claim: Jiang says everyone in this bolgia should be treated with suspicion because it is the circle of fraud and deception, so even apparently helpful speech is probably a trick.
He reads the sinner's proposal to summon seven more grafters as a tactical lie that exploits the demons' appetite for more victims.

Jiang introduces a rule of hell for this discussion: when damned souls address Dante and Virgil directly, their words are supposed to be true, which creates a contradiction when this sinner appears to lie.
The packet's paradox is that demons get punished for believing a liar in the realm of fraud, while the liar seems momentarily to succeed by manipulating their own violent instincts.

signature_moments.moment: Fraud becomes recursive here: a condemned trickster bargains for a few seconds of mercy by promising seven new victims to torturers who love being tricked into more cruelty.
signature_moments.source_phrase: i'll trick seven more to appear
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures the comic-serious density of the scene and Jiang's insistence that every move in this circle is contaminated by deception.

signature_moments.moment: Hell contains a contradiction: the sinner lies, yet Jiang says the damned are supposed to tell Dante and Virgil the truth.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you cannot lie to virgil and dante
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This paradox drives the next interpretive move and shows Jiang reading the canto as a puzzle rather than a flat morality tale.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's reminder that this bolgia should be read as an environment where speech, bargains, and appearances are systematically deceptive.
Jiang's stated interpretive rule that souls in hell cannot simply lie when speaking to Dante and Virgil, which makes this episode paradoxical.

uncertainty_notes.note: The reading of names and proper nouns is heavily degraded by ASR, but the narrative function is still clear: the sinner identifies other corrupt figures and bargains to expose more if the demons step back.
